2. Habitat Alteration
Excavation of the stream channels during the winter period would create a total disturbance to existing stream habitat. The significance 
of these impacts to the creeks within the Sikanni Chief drainage (Lapp, Unnamed to Gutah and Gutah creeks) will likely be low due to 
the limited habitat capabilities for salmonid fish species at these crossing sites. These crossing sites would be restored to 
preconstruction conditions using native materials salvaged from the crossing sites. The presence of a wide unconstricted floodplain at 
the crossing sites and the fact that these creeks are low energy systems (low channel gradient and wide floodplain areas) suggest that 
bank erosion would not be a major concern at these crossing sites. 
Assuming that the crossings of the Black and Birley creek sites (Beatton River drainage) can be completed with a non-intrusive 
crossing method (horizontal bore or directional drill) there would be no impact to instream habitat capabilities. However, in the event 
that the contingency crossing method is required for one or both of these crossings, there could be a significant impact to existing 
habitat capabilities for Arctic grayling and possibly other high priority fish species that are likely present at these crossing sites. 
Habitat values at these crossing sites would be restored by reconstructing the channel with salvaged cobble materials, when available, 
and by installing tree revetments along the disturbed portion of the banks on one side of the creek at each crossing location. These 
measures will ensure that existing rearing and over-wintering habitat capabilities are maintained at the crossing sites.

3. Water Quality
Maintenance of downstream water quality during the construction period would be an important consideration for fish habitat 
protection at the Black and Birley creek crossing sites, the lower reaches of these systems, as well as in the mainstem Beatton River. A 
high level of water quality protection will be achieved if the non-intrusive crossing methods can be achieved. There would be some 
risk of water quality degradation during the construction period if the contingency crossing method (dam and pump) is required at 
either of these two sites. This risk can be reduced by ensuring that the adequate dams seals are obtained and that sufficient pumping 
capacity is on-site. These measures would also apply to the three tributary crossings in the Sikanni Chief drainage (Lapp, Unnamed to 
Gutah and Gutah creeks).
There is also potential for longer term water quality impacts if disturbed portions of the banks are not adequately restored. This 
concern would apply to those creek crossings where open trenching has occurred. The risk of these potential impacts would be reduced 
by ensuring that the disturbed banks are graded to a stable condition and that adequate re-vegetation of the sites in achieved (refer to 
Section 7.8.4). Grading and stock piling the coarser sized material for use in bank construction would assist in the stabilization of the 
stream banks.

4. Vegetation Clearing
With the exception of Crossing Site RGG1 on Black Creek, all of the crossing sites are characterized by an absence of tree growth in 
the immediate riparian zone. ROW clearing requirements at these sites will have little, if any, impact on existing fish habitat 
capabilities at the crossing sites. There may be some impact if ROW clearing is required within the existing riparian zone at the Black 
Creek crossing site (contingency crossing method only). This potential impact the Back Creek crossing site would be minimized by 
ensuring that the width of the clearing is kept to a minimum and that grubbing would be restricted to the width of the trench on both 
sides of the creek at the crossing location. 
Re-establishment of riparian vegetation on the stream banks at each crossing site will be required to promote long term site stability 
and minimize erosion potential from the disturbed banks.

5. Approach Slope Stability
All of the creek crossings are characterized by low lying floodplain areas and there are no approach slopes to contend with. There is no 
potential for slumping adjacent to the creek beds. Provisions for drainage across the ROW and re-seeding the disturbed areas will 
alleviate any potential erosion problems near the creek crossings.

3. Water Quality
Water quality impacts at not anticipated for any of the tributary crossing work due to the winter construction schedule and the high 
probability that all water would be frozen solid to the stream beds. One possible exception would be crossing GT8 on the unnamed 
tributary marsh to Aitken Creek. This site is characterized by an extensive network of marsh ponds and standing water may be present. 
Silt screens or pumps would be used at this site to contain sediment disturbed during construction if required. It is unlikely that there 
would be significant sediment related impacts from this work to downstream habitat since there are large pond areas immediately 
downstream of the crossing site that would provide a suitable settling area before any flowing water reaches fish bearing waters.

4. Vegetation
Additional vegetation clearing would be required adjacent to the tributary crossings along the existing ROW. This clearing would have 
no direct impact to fish habitat but could increase erosion potential with a possible negative effect on downstream water quality. For 
this reason it is proposed that all stream side clearing of mature tress be minimized wherever possible. 
No additional vegetation clearing is anticipated adjacent to the Beatton River crossing if the proposed directional drill crossing is 
successful.

5. Approach Slope Stability
All of the crossing sites are characterized by wide, extensive floodplain areas with no significant grade. Mass wasting and/or slumping 
is not anticipated on any of the creek approaches. There is the some potential for additional erosion of the ROW adjacent to the creeks 
and water runs. This potential is highest at crossing sites GT5, GT10, GT11 and GT12 all of which have significant erosion problems 
on the ROW associated with the existing pipeline. Provisions for drainage across the ROW and re-seeding the disturbed areas will 
alleviate any potential erosion problems near the creek crossings.

6. Proposed Stream Crossing Techniques
With the exception of the Beatton River crossing, all of the affected streams are small headwater drainages characterized by low 
summer flow volumes. All of the creeks and water runs affected, with the possible exception of the Blueberry River and Nig Creek 
sites, are expected to be frozen solid during the construction period. It is proposed that these crossings would be completed using an 
open-cut crossing technique (winter construction only). In the event that water is present at any of the crossing sites, then the dam and 
pump crossing technique would be implemented as a contingency crossing technique. The dam and pump crossing method is proposed 
as the primary crossing method for the Blueberry River (GT1) and Nig Creek (GT11) crossing sites. In the event that there is no water 
present at the time of construction, then an open-cut crossing would be used at these two sites. Given the expected conditions of these 
crossing sites during the winter period and the low fisheries values associated with the sites, it is unlikely that the proposed work 
would have any impact to fish resources. The proposed crossing methods would result in "dry" instream work and there would be low 
risk to downstream water quality and fish habitat. Silt screens and pumps would be used to ensure the work site is isolated at these 
crossing sites if standing or flowing water is present at the time of construction. 
Due to high fisheries values, including the high probability of over-wintering fish, and the presence of a highly instable bank at the 
Beatton River crossing sites (GT14 and GT14A), a directional drill crossing is proposed as the main crossing method for these sites. In 
the event that the directional drill crossing is not successful then a dam and pump crossing with complete work site isolation would be 
used at this location.
7.8.4 Environmental Mitigation and Monitoring
7.8.4.1 Fish Salvage
Crossing sites where fish salvage is required, or may possibly be required, are identified for the two pipeline routes below. If fish 
salvage work was required at any of these sites it would be necessary to remove all fish with an electrofisher and seine nets after the 
ice cover had been removed and prior to any instream construction work. This work would be done by the Environmental Inspector. 
All appropriate fish salvage permits would be obtained prior to the project.

1. Raw Gas Gathering Pipeline
There is moderate to high potential that over-wintering fish would be present at the Black and Birley creek crossing sites (RGG1 and 
RGG2). However, fish salvage would only be required at these two sites in the contingency crossing method (dam and pump) was 
implemented. No fish salvage would be required at these sites if the horizontal bore or directional drill crossing methods are 
successfully implemented. It is unlikely that fish salvage would be required at the three crossing sites in the Lapp and Gutah creek 
drainages (crossing sites RGG3, RGG4 and RGG5).

2. Raw Gas Transmission Pipeline
Fish salvage would not be required at any of the tributary crossings of the Beatton River. Fish were not found at any of these sites 
during the summer period and over-wintering habitat capabilities are low to non-nonexistent at these sites. 
The only site where fish salvage may be required would be the Beatton River crossing (GT14). Fish salvage at this site would only be 
required if the contingency crossing method (dam and pump) was used.
7.8.4.2 Work Site Isolation
The proposed crossing methods have been selected to ensure total work site isolation at the crossing locations. Site specific 
requirements for work site isolation measures are discussed for the two pipeline routes below.

1. Raw Gas Gathering Pipeline
There would be no instream work required for the Black and Birley creek crossing sites since horizontal bore or directional drill 
crossings are proposed. Complete work site isolation is proposed for the other three crossings in the Lapp and Gutah creek drainages 
(Sites RGG3, RGG4 and RGG5) along this route. Complete work site isolation would also be implemented at the Black and Birley 
Creek sites if the contingency crossing method (dam and pump) is required at either of these sites.

2. Raw Gas Transmission Pipeline
In most cases it is anticipated that all water in the affected tributary drainages of the Beatton River would be frozen during the 
construction period. For those crossing sites where water may be present (GT1 ,GT8 and GT11) during the proposed winter 
construction period then measures would be implemented to ensure complete work site isolation. This would include the use of poly 
sealed dams and pumps. Silt screens and natural settling areas would be used at crossing site GT8 if required. 
If a dam and pump crossing method is implemented for the Beatton River crossing (contingency only), then special measures would be 
required at this site to ensure a complete seal of the work site. These measures would include the removal of all ice cover, selective 
removal of all large rocks at the proposed dam sites, installation of a poly seal and placement of bulk sand bags across the channel. 
7.8.4.3 Contingency Crossing Plans (Both Routes)
The proposed stream crossing methods have been selected on the basis of environmental protection objectives and anticipated site 
conditions during the winter period. Although there is a high probability that the proposed crossing methods will be effective for the 
crossing work, contingency crossing plans have been proposed in case site conditions are different from those anticipated. Table 7.8-1 
summarizes the proposed and alternate crossing methods for each of the previously described stream crossings.

The main variable would be the possible presence of flowing water at the tributary crossing sites. In all cases, including the Beatton 
River crossing, the dam and pump crossing method has been proposed as the contingency crossing plan. Possible implementation of 
the contingency crossing plan at the tributary sites would be evaluated by the Environmental Inspector for the job (see below). The 
regulatory agencies would be consulted in the event that the contingency crossing plan was required for the Beatton River crossing.
7.8.4.4 Clearing and Grubbing (Both Routes)
Creek side clearing and grubbing would not be required at crossings where a directional drill of horizontal bore crossing technique is 
proposed. These crossings include the Black and Birley creek sites (RGG1 and RGG2) on the raw Gas Gathering Pipeline and the 
Beatton River crossing (GT14) on the Raw Gas Transmission Pipeline. Creek side clearing and grubbing would only be required at 
these sites if the contingency crossing method (dam and pump) was required.
It is proposed that riparian clearing be minimized at all crossing sites on both routes and that creek site grubbing be restricted to the 
width of the pipe trench in all cases. This measure will promote bank stability and re-generation potential be leaving the root stock of 
any removed trees in place. 
7.8.4.5 Bank Reconstruction
Bank reconstruction measures would be implemented at all sites to ensure that existing habitat capabilities are preserved and to 
promote site stability and the resultant protection of downstream water qual

1. Raw Gas Gathering Pipeline
All of the affected tributary streams to the Sikanni Chief River along this route (Lapp and Gutah creek crossing sites) are low energy 
systems and extensive bank reconstruction work (bank armouring) is not anticipated. Similarly, there is no evidence of extensive bank 
erosion at he Black and Birley creek crossing sites and rip rap armouring is not anticipated. The stream banks at these crossing 
locations would be graded to a stable slope and re-vegetated (refer to Section 7.8.4.6 below).

2.  Disturbed areas will be regraded (EPP Section E2.9). 
General Traditional Use:
· Issue: Keep owners of Registered Trapping Areas informed during all stages of the project, including planning, and advised well in 
advance of construction activities.
Mitigation Response: Included in project communications plans.
· Issue: Help eliminate poaching of valuable furbearers (e.g. lynx) from registered traplines that might occur as a result of increased 
access.
Mitigation Response: Project involves minimal new permanent access.
· Issue: Ensure that the burial grounds along the Chauvco line are not disturbed by project activities.
Mitigation Response: Has been considered in choosing pipeline route.
· Issue: Avoid archaeologically sensitive sites when locating right-of-ways.
Mitigation Response: Has been addressed through archaeological assessment and pipeline construction plan and route.
· Issue: Avoid wildlife habitat when locating right-of-ways.
Mitigation Response: Impact on habitat minimized through route selection process.
· Issue: Employ one or more environmental monitors, preferably Band members during clearing and construction to ensure that the 
exact locations of game trails and other significant traditional use sites intersected by the pipeline routing remain clearly marked, and 
to ensure that appropriate mitigative measures are employed.
Mitigation Response: Addressed in Section E2.1 of EPP.
Safety:
· Issue: Prevent non-Native project workers from carrying firearms.
Mitigation Response: Addressed in Section E2.11 of EPP.
